newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Congress raises fresh doubts on NATO.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Congress raises fresh doubts on NATO.

text.p: With its focus now on striking an accommodation with Russia, the Clinton administration on Wednesday faced new doubts in Congress about expanding NATO eastward to include ex-communist states.

At a hearing with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, influential Democratic Representative David Obey of Wisconsin blasted the enlargement plans which are President Bill Clinton's main national security priority this year, calling them a "historically arrogant decision which we will come to regret."

Meanwhile Republican Representative Ralph Regula of Ohio argued that it would be more appropriate, and effective, for the European Union, rather than NATO, to be the first to take in the former communist states as members.
He urged that EU membership be made a precondition of NATO membership, but Albright, testifying before the House Appropriations subcommittee on state, commerce and justice, opposed that idea.

The United States is leading the alliance campaign for expansion, which faces a crucial moment at a July NATO summit in Madrid when the first post-Cold War invitations to ex-communist states are to be issued.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are the top contenders, but Romania and Slovenia are under discussion.
As part of that effort, NATO is also negotiating with Russia a sweetner package designed to calm Moscow's fears about expansion.

It includes promises of significant conventional arms reductions in Europe and a charter or other document that would define Russia-NATO ties and ensure a permanent mechanism -- a joint council -- for regular dialogue and cooperation.
Albright discussed the package in Moscow with President Boris Yeltsin two weeks ago and Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott was holding more talks in Moscow this week.
U.S. officials hope there will be concrete progress on this thorny issue at the March 20-21 summit in Helsinki between Clinton and Yeltsin.

In her testimony, Albright again made the case for NATO expansion, saying it was part of an effort to "ensure NATO's continued role as a mighty instrument for peace, stability and freedom throughout Europe." It would envelope "new democracies as part of a security system," she said.

If Eastern European countries were not admitted to NATO, they would have been punished twice, first by being cut off from the West after the Second World War and then also by being excluded from NATO in the post-Cold War era, said Albright, who was born in Czechoslovakia.

But Obey voiced "profound misgivings." He said he feared Russian nationalists would exploit any expansion-related deal Moscow concludes with the alliance and that Americans did not really understand the consequences of expansion, which call for NATO to go to war if any of its members are attacked.
He expressed concern that expansion would create new divisions in Europe and make it harder to win Russian parliament approval of START 2, the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty.

Regula peppered Albright with questions about the need for expansion and said "it seems to me the first step ought to be the expansion of the European Union to include these countries because they need economic development."
Albright said "we are doing both ... (and) we believe both are important, but the NATO alliance unanimously had decided that it was a good idea to move forward with NATO enlargement."

She stressed that the United States was part of NATO, not of the EU, but had urged the EU to include the new democracies as members. The NATO expansion decision was made for its own sake to get rid of the "gray zone" created in central and eastern Europe, she said.
"I think that it's important to move forward with both but not make one a pre-condition to the other," she said.
